before.quote: The silver men talk sense about what's crushing the farm prices. The gold standard's been hard on men like us, and this candidate means to do something about it right away.
before.reason: Harry Hill is a 26-year-old white man in rural Ohio with voting rights. The recent newspaper accounts he has read extensively discuss the silver coinage debate and its effects on agricultural prices and the debtor class—issues directly affecting his farming livelihood. The free-silver platform of Bryan, endorsed by the farmer-labor coalition and promising action without waiting for international agreement, aligns with the monetary relief arguments made in the sources he has encountered.

after.quote: The price of wheat keeps falling while what I owe stays the same. Free silver might help us farmers get a better price for our crop come next year.
after.reason: Harry Hill is a wheat farmer in Ohio facing sharply depressed crop prices and mounting debt burdens in October 1896. He has read arguments in his local press that free silver coinage would increase the money supply, raise prices, and ease the debt burden on farmers—making him responsive to Bryan's platform of unlimited silver coinage and opposition to bond sales defending the gold standard. He is likely to vote and likely to support Bryan.

before.quote: The free silver talk sounds fine, but I've read enough to know it'll wreck the currency. The Republican's got the right idea on honest money and keeping jobs at home.
before.reason: Ernest Reed is a mill or railroad worker in Massachusetts who has been exposed to arguments against free silver as financially ruinous, particularly from labor perspectives. The articles he has read emphasize gold standard stability and warn against free coinage's dangers, while McKinley promises protective tariffs and labor arbitration—both appealing to his economic interests as a wage earner.

after.quote: The Democrats talk free silver like it'll fix everything, but I've read it ruined Mexico. A good tariff and steady money is what keeps the mills running and the work steady.
after.reason: Ernest Reed is a mill or railroad worker in Massachusetts whose household depends on industrial wages. The falling wheat prices and currency debates have reached him through newspaper accounts linking silver coinage to market instability. McKinley's platform of protective tariff and labor arbitration appeals to his class interests, though the free-silver movement's promise of debt relief holds some pull.

before.quote: I cannot vote tomorrow, though I hear plenty about what the men will choose. My husband will decide how our household's vote goes.

after.quote: I wish I could vote tomorrow. The wheat prices have been dreadful, and I've read enough to know where I'd stand on the money question.
after.reason: Helen Dawson is a woman in Indiana in 1896, and women are barred by law from voting for president. She cannot cast a ballot regardless of her views on the currency, tariff, or labor questions.

before.quote: I cannot vote myself, but my husband and sons will cast their ballots tomorrow. Times are hard for us farmers with these low prices.

after.quote: I cannot vote myself, but my husband knows well enough what the falling wheat prices mean for us. We are deeper in debt each year.

wheat-prices-keep-falling.name: Samuel Carter
wheat-prices-keep-falling.line: 74, a city or town, New York

before.quote: The monopolies and the trusts have had their way long enough. We fought to free men from one kind of bondage—we must free them from the bankers' chains now.
before.reason: Samuel Carter is a 74-year-old man of business in New York with a long memory of the Civil War and the Republican Party of Lincoln and reform. The Journal article's invocation of Lincoln's fight against tyranny and government by special interests resonates with the free-silver platform's condemnation of bond sales to banking syndicates and government by injunction. At his age and station, he is likely to vote, though health or weather might prevent him.

after.quote: The farmers are being ruined by falling wheat prices and the gold men's policies. We need free silver and an end to government siding with the trusts against working people.
after.reason: Samuel Carter, at 74 with a business in New York, has witnessed the catastrophic wheat price collapse and understands the free-silver platform's appeal to agricultural interests and debtors, reinforced by the Journal's populist reform rhetoric he has read; yet his age, urban mercantile position, and exposure to the Tribune's economic concerns create some pull toward the gold-standard position.

before.quote: The railroads are bleeding us dry, and this gold money makes it worse. A man ought to have free silver to get a fair price for his cotton and his work.
before.reason: James Hayes is a farmer in Tennessee who has read recent arguments about free silver, railroad rates, and the gold standard's effects on agricultural producers. The sources he has encountered emphasize how gold policy and railroad combinations have harmed farmers' purchasing power and raised their costs, which aligns with Bryan's platform of free silver and criticism of banking syndicates.

after.quote: The wheat prices keep falling and the debts pile up. That man Bryan says he'll open the silver coinage and stop letting the bankers run things with their gold. That's what we need.
after.reason: Hayes is a wheat farmer in Tennessee facing sustained price collapse and mounting debt burdens, circumstances that align him with the free-silver platform of Bryan, who also condemns bond sales to banking syndicates and favors an income tax—positions addressing the financial distress afflicting farmers. Hayes can lawfully vote if he pays the poll tax, which a farming household would ordinarily manage.

before.quote: I cannot vote, being a woman—that's the law here in South Dakota. My husband will have to cast our ballot.
before.reason: Alice Tate is a woman in South Dakota in 1896, and women are legally barred from voting for president in that state. She cannot lawfully cast a ballot regardless of her preferences.

after.quote: I wish I could have a say in it, but women don't get to vote here. My husband will have to cast the ballot for us.
after.reason: Alice Tate is a woman in South Dakota in 1896, and women are not permitted to vote for president in this state. Her inability to vote is a legal barrier, not a matter of choice or circumstance.

before.quote: I can't vote myself, but my husband will be going to the polls tomorrow. I've heard plenty about what the candidates stand for.
before.reason: Ruth Robinson is a white woman born in the United States living in New York in 1896. The brief explicitly states that women cannot vote for president in New York, making her ineligible to cast a ballot regardless of her views on the candidates or issues.

after.quote: I cannot vote in this election—women have no say in presidential elections here. But my husband will be voting, and we've discussed what's best for our farm.
after.reason: Ruth Robinson is a woman in New York in 1896, and women cannot vote for president in this state. Her legal inability to vote is absolute regardless of her preferences or circumstances.

before.quote: The free-silver man seems to understand what's been squeezing us working folks—those bond sales to the bankers and the way they use injunctions against us. That makes more sense to me than the gold standard crowd.
before.reason: Harry Tate works in a mill, shop, mine or railroad in Illinois and has read recent newspaper discussion of the silver question and the government's bond sales to banking syndicates. Bryan's platform directly opposes those bond sales, supports free silver coinage, and condemns government by injunction against strikers—positions aligned with a working man's economic interests and grievances, though the novelty of the free-silver break with the incumbent administration leaves some uncertainty.

after.quote: The farmer's in trouble, and that means work dries up for us too. Silver's the answer they say, and at least Bryan is fighting the banks instead of helping them.
after.reason: Harry Tate works on mill or railroad wages in Illinois during severe agricultural depression; wheat prices have collapsed and farm debt burdens have worsened, creating economic distress that extends to wage-earning households. The free-silver platform directly addresses the monetary contraction and gold standard policies that workers and farmers blame for hard times, while opposing the bond sales and injunctions against strikers that have harmed working people.

before.quote: Free silver is what we need out here—the gold standard is strangling us. That fellow Bryan understands what's happened to farm prices and who's to blame.
before.reason: George Irwin is a farmer in Texas during an economic depression caused by what he reads as the gold standard's failure. The free-silver platform directly addresses agrarian distress through currency inflation that would ease debt burdens and raise crop prices, while the protective tariff and income tax proposals align with farmer interests against eastern banking syndicates.

after.quote: The silver man's got the right idea about what's broken our backs. These prices are killing us, and somebody's got to answer for it.
after.reason: George Irwin is a wheat farmer in Texas facing collapsing prices and mounting debt burdens in 1896. Bryan's free-silver platform and opposition to bond sales to banking syndicates directly address the monetary pressures crushing agricultural producers, while his income tax and tariff-for-revenue stance align with farmer interests against industrial protection.

reading.summary: Argues bimetallism is more stable and just than a gold standard.
A former resident who lived in Mexico urges laboring men to oppose free silver.
Railroad rate notices for lumber and leather shipments, effective September 6.
Argues free coinage would not swamp mints; silver would be stored behind certificates.
Viceroy's party tours the Treasury vaults, showing interest in the bond issue division.
Treasurer's report discusses net gold balances after redemptions began and export supply.
Argues restoring silver would lessen gold demand and change the dollar's purchasing power.
Argues the gold standard burdens farmers with fixed debts and wage earners.
Argues free silver would hurt workingmen, whose wages rest on gold coin.
Treasury sold $262 million in bonds for gold to replenish the reserve.
Speaker says reformers are always called revolutionists, citing Lincoln, and urges standing by principles.
Argues the gold standard has effectively doubled railroad rates, naming Morgan.
Cites Cleveland's messages describing greenback redemption as an endless chain draining the Treasury's gold.
Writer predicts free coinage would drop silver to market value, citing Mexican dollars.
Discusses how gold value and currency uncertainty affected wheat prices in several markets.
Speaker attacks foreign money changers; says St. Louis banks withheld gold from customers.
Argues bondholders cannot demand gold under Congress's resolution, though bonds were paid in gold.
Speaker mocks sudden defenders of the income tax decision, who would pay it.
Speaker says gold-standard men adopted a bimetallist platform at St. Louis.
Partly legible wheat price table and talk of whether bread prices follow wheat.
Speaker cites Senator Howe's defense of the income tax and criticizes the Supreme Court.
